utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we hear the testimony of the next witness, a few procedural matters. Mr. Carrier, we tried to find out whether there were any protective measures sought, and I'm also addressing the Defence. Apparently, there's no request for protective measures for the next witness. Then the second item: I'd like to put on the record that on the 25th of February, Chamber staff has informed the parties by e-mail of the intended scope of the examination-in-chief of Witness Juric. The e-mail reads, in the relevant parts, as follows: "First, the Chamber intends to question Witness CW-2," as he was still called then, "about his role in Sector South between approximately the 3rd and the 13th of August, 1995. The Chamber may ask the witness specific questions concerning his appointment and authority. "Second, the Chamber intends to question Witness CW-2 about his knowledge and sources of his knowledge of events on the ground in the context of the reporting system. "Third, the Chamber intends to question Witness CW-2 on some aspects of the relation of the military police with other civilian and military authorities, including the Special Police. The Chamber does not intend to examine Witness CW-2 on the functioning and structure of the military police in general, other than stated above." I move on to the next issue. On the 4th of February, 2010, the Gotovina Defence filed a stipulation to portions of the Prosecution's pre-trial brief in which the Gotovina Defence stipulated to paragraphs 105 to 108 of the OTP's pre-trial brief, except to the second sentence of paragraph 105, to the extent it implies that the armed conflict in 1991 was initiated by the Croatian government. On the 26th of February, the Cermak Defence joined the stipulation, which is found at transcript page 27.399. On the 28th of February, the Markac Defence informally informed the Chamber that it would not join the above-mentioned stipulation due to its position that the armed conflict within the territorial scope of the indictment ceased on or about the 8th of August, 1995. The Trial Chamber wanted this to be put on the record and asks the Markac Defence whether it joins the stipulation, except insofar as it implies that the armed conflict continued beyond the 8th of August. Mr. Mikulicic, I'm addressing you, because it seems that the Markac Defence main concern is whether the mop-up operations are still part of the armed conflict. Therefore, the Chamber wondered, but we'd like to hear from you, whether on the remainder -- on other aspects of the stipulation, you would still join -- or at least that we would know to what extent you challenge what is found in the other parts of the paragraphs where the Gotovina Defence and the Cermak Defence jointly made their stipulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. First of all, good morning, Your Honour, and everybody in the courtroom. Indeed, Your Honour, the main concern of the Markac Defence is exactly what you pointed out. As it regards to the rest of the stipulation subject, we have no problem with it. So our main concern is the statement that the armed conflict has ceased from the or about 8th of August, 1995. So as it regards to the other part of opening brief of the Prosecution which the Gotovina Defence would like to stipulate, we have no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any way that you could very precisely define what is and what is not agreed upon?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'll try to do that. But the wording of that paragraph pointed out by the Gotovina Defence from the opening trial brief, the wording is such -- in such a manner that it's very complex, and then I simply cannot exchange one sentence from, let's say, paragraph 107, and as it regards to the other paragraphs, that sentence is some way stipulated in the other form of the paragraphs. So I don't think I could do that, I don't think. I tried to follow the guidance of the Trial Chamber and just to focus on the main subject, but the wording of that paragraph are so, I would say, complex that I simply cannot extract one part of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can imagine that there are other aspects on which -- whether or not you follow verbatim the wording of the OTP's pre-trial brief, that there are other parts on which you could agree perhaps in free language. For example, it might clarify issues as whether the Markac Defence considered the armed conflict as an international or a non-international armed conflict. There are a few other parts remaining on which you may seek agreement and which would not contradict the stipulations as they were made by the Gotovina and the Cermak Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we could easily do that, and we could easily address the Chamber and the other parties with our position as it regards. But as I said, the wording of that paragraphs are simply not easy to be stipulated in totality, so I have to express what position is from Markac Defence as it regards to the other part of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Even if you would not follow literally every word --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- then, nevertheless, it may -- it may assist in the Chamber in establishing that some matters are not contested, even if you do not follow verbatim the text of paragraphs 105 and 108, and you're encouraged to see what can be done in this --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We will proceed that way, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then having dealt with those procedural issues, is there anything else? Otherwise, I would like the witness to be brought into the courtroom. When later today I refer to pages of documents, I will always refer to the e-court page numbers and not the page numbers on the hard copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Juric. Mr. Juric, before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration, the text of which is now handed out to you by the usher, and I would like -- yes. You were not able to follow my first words. You had not your earphones on. I'll then repeat what I said. Mr. Juric, before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration, the text of which is now handed out to you by Madam Usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Juric. Please be seated. Mr. Juric, you'll first be examined by the Chamber. Then the Prosecution will put further questions to you. And after that, you'll be

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Juric, could you, first of all, state your full name and date of birth for the record?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ivan Juric. I was born on the 28th of October, 1963.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Juric, could you tell us what your present job is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm the commander of the Command for Doctrine, Fran Krsto Frankopan, affiliated with the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what is your rank in the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a brigadier general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you also tell us what your military rank was in the first half of August 1995; that is, during Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, I was a member of the Administration of the Military Police, and my rank was major.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you kept that rank until ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Up to the end of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Juric, in some of the questions the Chamber will rely on the evidence it has already received, not to say that if you disagree with that, please don't hesitate to tell us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you confirm that you arrived in the former Sector South on the 3rd of August, 1995, and that you left again around the 13th of August?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Juric, the indictment in this case alleges that during and after Operation Storm, crimes were committed by Croatian military and police forces against the population of Serb ethnicity living in the Krajina region in a period which did include August 1995. During your mission in the field, did you receive any information that crimes, such as looting, burning, killings and mistreatment, were committed by the HV or by the MUP Special Police, members of the HV and members of the MUP Special Police?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: I can't say with any certainty what form of information I received when I was in the field. However, I am sure that I did receive a couple of pieces of information that some members of either the armed forces or individuals wearing parts of the uniform or without uniform were involved in some illegal acts. However, I can say with 100 per cent certainty that I did not receive information about any major crimes, as it were, being committed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two follow-up questions. When you talk about the armed forces, that would include what forces exactly?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Members of the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You do not include members of MUP forces or Special Police forces which may have taken part in operational --

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does that mean that you received information only about HV members and individuals wearing uniforms, or did you also receive information about possible crimes committed by police or Special Police forces?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I did not receive information about any crimes that might have been committed by members of either the civilian police or the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was talking about civilian police -- about MUP forces, I earlier said, and Special Police forces. I had not yet mentioned military police forces. So we have --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was going to rise because I think we needed to check the interpretation of the last police force that he mentioned on page 8, line 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When you said you did not receive information about any crimes that might have been committed by members of either the civilian police or -- what did you then say? What other police force did you mention; Special Police, military police?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: The civilian police or the Special Police. These are the terms that we use, and imply the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, as far as military police is concerned, did you receive any reports about crimes that may have been committed by members of the military police?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us in a bit more detail, as you said before, of these crimes committed? I think you excluded major crimes. You said: "I can say with 100 per cent certainty that I did not receive information about any major crimes being committed." Now, what do you consider to be major crimes?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: That some killings were committed somewhere, that there were major violations of military discipline. In any case, had I received such information, I would have remembered it. But whatever information we received on the happenings on the ground, we tried to act upon it and deal with the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, in my question, I included burning, looting, killings. Would you consider all of these not to be major crimes or did you not receive any information about such crimes?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: No, I did not receive information about such crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could you explain to us what illegal acts you were talking about when you said that you received some information? You said: "A couple of pieces of information that some members of either the armed forces or individuals wearing parts of uniforms or without uniforms were involved in some illegal acts." What illegal acts and what pieces of information did you refer to?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: That mostly concerns information that I received from the commander of the 72nd and 73rd Battalion of the Military Police about the work of their members at check-points, and the work and what they noted during their patrols across certain areas. The whole area of responsibility was very big. We had very few people at our disposal. At the check-points, they stopped everybody who entered or left the area of responsibility at the places where we, as members of the military police, found ourselves. And as we inspected them and their personal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll stop you there. You're explaining on what was the situation in which information could be received. Could you tell us what illegal acts, then, were -- came to your knowledge at the time, if not looting, burning, killing? What kind of illegal acts do we have to think about or, as a matter of fact, you referred to in your answer?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Certain individuals who came to the check-point were in possession of some objects that they could not prove that they rightfully belonged to them, and we seized those things. I can't say whether those objects were obtained by looting or -- most of them said that those things belonged to them or had belonged to them. In any case, all those objects were seized and handed over -- I can't remember exactly where. There was a reception centre that was organised by the civilian structures of authority that received all those goods, cattle, or whatever was found in the possession of those individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That reception centre was situated where?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really can't say with 100 per cent certainty. I can't answer. I know that one was in the area of Zadar -- in the region of Zadar, another one in the region of Sibenik, and I believe that one was in the region of Sinj, but I'm not 100 per cent sure of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Until now, we talked about illegal acts, and my question was also about crimes that were reported. Did you personally witness any crimes committed by Croatian forces during your posting in Sector South in this period between the 3rd and the 13th of August?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, not me, personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will then move on. Mr. Juric, is it correct that in the first half of August 1995, you were posted to the area where Operation Storm took place, pursuant to an order of General Lausic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us what your specific tasks were and what the area of responsibility was in the former Sector South in this period of time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Together with a team of officers from the Administration of the Military Police, I was sent to the area of Split and to cover the area of responsibility of Split Military District, and co-ordinate the work of the 72nd and the 73rd Battalions of the Military Police in their joint work. And together with the team, I was supposed to extend professional support to the military police in co-ordination and co-ordinated work of the military police, civilian police, members of the SIS, and all other security services, if you will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us exactly when you arrived in Knin?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: I think it was on the second day of the operation, around 6.00 or 7.00 or 8.00 in the evening. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it be the 5th?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: That would be the 5th, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as your authority is concerned, Mr. Juric, could you tell us, in this period of time between the 3rd and the 13th of August, did you have authority over the commanders of the 72nd and 73rd Military Police Battalions?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: In principle, the orders that I received, and as I received these orders, in a way, I was the superior of the commanders of the 72nd and 73rd within the part of their tasks where they had joint activities to carry out. As far as the military police is concerned, I had the right to issue orders to them, but I don't think I was their superior in the formal or legal sense of the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could ask the witness again to repeat part of his answer. At page 12, line 3, I believe he made a reference to from where his authority flowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you answer the question? And you told us that you were superior to the commanders of the 72nd and 73rd within the part of their tasks, as you said, where they had joint activities to carry out. And then you continued by saying: "As far as the military police is concerned ..." And could you then repeat what you then said, what right you had?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: I said that I had authority from the Administration of the Military Police, and that on that basis I could give them tasks. But from a formal and legal point of view, I was not their superior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you further explain what you mean exactly with: "I had authority from the Administration of the Military Police"?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: The Military Police Administration was the superior of units. I was head of the Traffic Department in the Military Police Administration, and on the basis of the position I held, the job I held, where I came from, and on the basis of the order of the chief of the Military Police Administration, I had this authority in terms of issuing orders or tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is it true that General Lausic delegated some of his powers to you on the basis of the existing legislation?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have --

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Could you perhaps give me an example?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm at this moment talking rather in the abstract, and the question was focusing on the powers General Lausic had under the order of the Croatian Ministry of Defence concerning the military police which was issued in 1994. The question was whether some of the powers were delegated to you by General Lausic.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you are speaking about the Rules of Service of the Military Police. Do you mean whether I got any powers from General Lausic on the basis of those rules? Is that what you're asking?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether he delegated part of his powers to you by appointing you.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Only what General Lausic wrote in his order when he sent me down there, and in the way in which I received that task and explained to him how and in which way I understood the task he gave me, but he could not have transferred any of his own powers or did I have any specific powers that the chief of the Military Police Administration had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me move on. I asked you to explain to us -- I asked you to explain what you meant exactly by: "I had authority from the Administration of the Military Police." Now, were you -- and I'm seeking further explanation of another part of your answer. Were you superior to the commanders of the 72nd and the 73rd Battalion of the Military Police; the 73rd to the extent that they assisted the 72nd? Were you superior to those commanders?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can say that partly, yes, to the extent to which they acted in co-ordinated fashion, but only in terms of that co-ordination, this co-ordinated activity, to work on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that your focus was on co-ordination, but could you give orders, then, to these military police battalion commanders, if need be?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: I would say tasks, that I issued tasks to them, and they were supposed to carry them out and to co-ordinate them. I did not write or issue any direct orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but if you give a task to someone who's then under an obligation to fulfill such a task, is that -- whether you call it orders or not is another matter, but what you said, they would have to do -- they would have to do it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I did not have any personal powers that an original commander has and that we can say that a commander has in general. I only had partial powers related to the execution of particular tasks. Specifically, I did not have any powers in the domain of personnel, and I could not do anything in that regard in these units. I only had something to do with the execution of the particular task involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have a look at D268. Mr. Juric, the texts will appear on your screen. If, however, you would feel the need to read a hard copy of a text, please ask us, and then we'll provide you with a hard copy. Could I have D268; page 2 in English, page 1 in B/C/S. Mr. Juric, you see the original on the screen. Perhaps enlarge it a bit so that you can better see it. Do you recognise this order?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We see, among other matters -- perhaps we go through it in the several elements. First of all, it reads that in the command system, that the commanders of the 72nd and the 73rd, in some respects, that you are superior to the commanders of those battalions. We discussed that already. If you have any further comment on that, please give it.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I can repeat what I've said. I really haven't seen this order in a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's no need to repeat anything. But since you have now the text in front of you, I wanted to give you an opportunity to add anything to your previous answer. Now, the second bullet point says that you are responsible for the implementation of all military police tasks in the 72nd Military Police Battalion zone of responsibility. That sounds as if your responsibility is unrestricted in respect of all military police tasks.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, but if you look at the first bullet point, you will see that it says that in the command system, I am superior to the commanders of the 72nd and 73rd Battalions with regard to extending assistance to the 72nd Battalion; that is to say, that it says explicitly that I am superior to these commanders only in that part of their tasks that pertain to assistance, as for the responsibility of carrying out all military police tasks in the area of responsibility of the 72nd Battalion, in terms of co-ordinating supervision and control of the implementation of tasks. However, by the time I got down there, almost all plans had already been worked out, and the commanders only told me how and in which way they carried out this planning, how and in which way the tasks would be carried out in stages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I read the first bullet point, but please correct me when my understanding is wrong, that the superiority over the commander of the 73rd Battalion is limited; however, not vice versa, that is, that your superiority to the commander of the 72nd would be also limited in the other direction of assistance. If my question is not clear, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I'm telling you now is how I understood the order or task at the time, and I then expressed that particular understanding of the order. I still claim that I did not have full command responsibility over the 72nd and 73rd Battalion of the Military Police or did I get that kind of transfer of authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In the semi-last bullet point, it reads that you are authorised to undertake all measures to ensure efficient and effective implementation of military police tasks in the 72nd Military Police Battalion and North OS zones of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I said that drawing on the authority of the Administration of Military Police, I did issue tasks to the members of the 72nd and 73rd Battalion of the Military Police, in terms to improve efficiency, methods, tactics, remove all observed shortcomings, and in order to carry out co-operation and co-ordination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your authority, would that be irrespective of the rank of the commanders of the 72nd and 73rd Military Police Battalions?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, could you tell us, were they higher in rank or were they not higher in rank compared to your rank, these commanders of the 72nd and 73rd?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: I think that all three of us held the same rank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, usually people of the same rank do not give orders to each other, isn't it? And that's what I meant with, irrespective of rank, that you would -- that you could give orders, although the commanders were not lower in rank.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Frankly speaking, I don't know what would have been the case had they held higher ranks than me. But I only considered them to be colleagues, and we worked on this job together, and that's why I keep saying that I issued them tasks rather than orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But even if they were of equal rank -- equal military rank to you, that did not negatively impact on your authority over them, being superior to them as commanders of the 72nd and 73rd?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: In the implementation of all of these tasks that we received and that we issued, they resolved that and they tried to resolve all of that on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you earlier said you could give them tasks and they had to fulfill those tasks. Now, you were of equal rank. The only thing I'm asking you, whether that in any way affected or negatively affected your authority, the fact that you were of equal rank, but, as you told us, you could, nevertheless, give them tasks and they had to perform those tasks?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: I don't think that it had any effect, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Juric, you have given an interview to investigators of the Office of the Prosecution in March 2002; is that -- can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, they conducted an interview. I don't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the last part of your sentence?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Yes. They conducted an interview with me, but I don't remember exactly when that occurred. I think that it was in the beginning of 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The date on the notes of the interview is that this interview took place on the 5th of March, 2002, which seems to be in line with your recollection. Could I just seek clarification of your statement, at least your statement as it was put on paper. I read off paragraph 26, where you said: "Two or three days ...," that's at least how it is reflected in the notes: "Two or three days after the president left Knin, I also left. I went out into the whole of the area that I was responsible for. I went to visit locations where the military police were situated. We were setting up military police posts in the liberated area. In some areas, we were tasked by other military police commanders to ensure the security of certain buildings." Could you tell us, "other military police commanders," to whom were you referring there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that there has been a mistake in the translation. I'm sure I didn't say "other military police commanders." When it came to providing security for certain facilities and certain parts in the liberated areas, we could only receive orders from our superiors. Whether they arrived from the Administration of the Military Police, the Main Staff, the Ministry of Defence, that's the institutions that I had in mind when talking about orders and who orders came from, and I suppose that that's what I said at that time. And I don't know why somebody decided to translate it with the words "military police." I'm sure that I didn't say that, because we didn't receive orders from the military police. I'm sure of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We are talking about, as it is put on paper, certain buildings, including two or three churches, electrical and water installations, and other parts of the infrastructure. So you say, When we received instructions to ensure the security of those buildings, those orders came from either the Administration of the Military Police, from the Main Staff, Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the that same interview, you are reported -- and I'm referring to paragraph 29, and I will read that to you. You're reported to have said: "During my time in the liberated area, I had no problems with the other military police commanders. I did not interfere with their jobs. I just tried to connect the work of the MUP and the military police. If there had been a problem, I would have informed General Lausic." Here, again, the wording, as we find it, is "other military police commanders." Could you tell us, in this context, to whom you referred?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know what the question was. But if we were talking about the area of responsibility, then we were talking exclusively about the commanders who were on the strength of the 72nd and the 73rd Battalions of the Military Police and were deployed in the area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You referred to your area of responsibility. How was that exactly defined? Was it defined by fixed geographical area or was it defined by the movement of other troops? Could you tell us what defined your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, at first the area of responsibility was the area of responsibility of the Split Military District. And as time went on, it followed the dynamics and the rate at which the units of the Croatian Army went on to liberate the occupied parts of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you would say it was a -- when they moved, your area of responsibility moved with their movements; is that how I have to understand?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, to a certain line that we considered the separation line between the combat area and the so-called non-combat area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, in Operation Storm, not only HV forces were operational, but other forces as well. For example, this Chamber received quite some information about the role of the Special Police in combat. Now, if the Special Police took part in the overall military Operation Storm, what influence would that have on your area of responsibility which, as you said, moved with the troops?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the military police did not have any authority over the Special Police. As far as I can remember, members of the Special Police participated in the performance of combat tasks in the area where I was in charge of the implementation of military police tasks. If my memory serves me well, I believe that to the left from us, in the direction of Lika, that's where they were deployed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To the left of you, you understand -- could you be a bit more precise? This Chamber received information - perhaps you could either confirm or challenge that - that, for example, the Special Police forces were moving from west to east, involved in the liberation of Gracac, then moved further east -- north-east to Donji Lapac. Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had that part in mind, but that was beyond my area of responsibility -- or, rather, it was not in my area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, if you exclude that, could you then be a bit more precise? Apparently, your authority moved with -- your area of responsibility moved with HV troops. Do we have to understand that there were no HV troops in that area; let us say, Gracac, and then on to Donji Lapac, Bruvno?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, as far as I can remember, that area of the Republic of Croatia did not belong to the part of the area of responsibility for which I was responsible in the implementation of military and police tasks. Therefore, I'm really not informed about the work and activities of the military police during Operation Storm. I didn't see them during Operation Storm. I didn't come across them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe page 22, line 11, he says he was not informed about the work and activities of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll ask the witness to repeat that. You told us that that that area of Croatia did not belong to the part of the area of responsibility for which you were responsible in the implementation of military and police tasks, and you then said: "Therefore, I'm really not informed about ..." And could you then please repeat what you then said? I think you said informed about the work and activities of -- of what, exactly?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: The work and activities of the Special Police during Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How did you know exactly where HV troops were operational and where they were not, because that apparently defined your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: We had meetings every day, and either I or the commander of the 72nd Battalion of the Military Police were present at those meetings. We were briefed about how far the units reached and how they had implemented their tasks. In principle, we learned, at that evening briefing, how far did the Croatian Army go in liberating that area the previous day, what lines they had reached, and that's how we knew where to set up our military and police check-points, what areas to patrol, up to a certain extent, up to the extent of the area where that was possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were there any mixed operations between the several parts of the armed forces, such as HV or police forces, taking part in Operation Storm; for example, troops moving on, receiving artillery support from other elements of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was a member of the military police. I did not participate in the planning and implementation of that type of operation, nor was I privy to that information. I was not familiar with that kind of operation, so I'm not in a position to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If your area of responsibility is defined by the movement of troops, I can imagine that it may have raised some questions as to your area of responsibility if operations were carried out by both HV and non-HV elements in the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. However, I repeat that we followed the units of the Croatian Army that were assigned to the Split Military District for the implementation of that task. The part where a special unit was deployed did not fall under the Split Military District, in terms of our responsibilities, so I would say that we exclusively followed those units that, according to our divisions, were assigned to the Split Military District.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I move to another subject, Mr. Juric. In performing your tasks, were you moving around on the ground?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us, how did you plan your movements, and what made you decide to go here or there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: It was mostly based on either reports received from subordinated officers attached to the 72nd Battalion of the Military Police, or parts of the 73rd Battalion, and those reports were relative to the organisation and establishment of new units of the military police, co-ordination, co-operation, the monitoring of the implementation of some of the tasks, the control of check-points, and how people manning check-points were performing their tasks. And in those terms, I did my planning as to where to go and how to make my inspections of the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for our impression - you spent approximately 10 days - what would be the distance you would travel on an average day?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did not make rounds of the units every day. It all depended on whether I had received some other tasks that I was supposed to carry out. On the 5th, we entered Knin. On the 6th, the president of Croatia, Mr. Tudjman, visited Knin, and I had a lot of work to do with regard to that, a lot of tasks. And I believe on the 7th, Mr. Yasushi Akashi came to Knin, which means that I had to be involved in providing security for him. And I believe that on the 8th or the 9th, or perhaps even on the 10th - I can't remember exactly - was when I carried out my first inspection of some elements of the units on the line stretching from Obrovac, Benkovac, Drnis, of that part, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Juric, the Chamber understands that you had a co-ordinating role in at least two respects; the first being the co-ordination between the 72nd and the 73rd Military Police Battalions, and the second co-ordinating role in respect of the work of the civil and the military police. Could you further explain to us what this co-ordination exactly was in both these areas, the first, 72nd and 73rd, and the other one, civilian and military police? Could we start with the first one, 72nd and 73rd, perhaps give us some examples on what exactly you then co-ordinated, how you co-ordinated.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Well, when the decision was being made about the engagement of the units of the military police in Operation Storm, due to the relatively small number of available police officers, the chief made a decision for the 73rd Battalion of the Military Police and its forces actively participated in the implementation of tasks in Operation Storm in the area of responsibility of the 72nd Battalion of the Military Police, which means that the 73rd Battalion of the Military Police, with some of its men, was involved in the work and activities that one could say were overlapping with the area of responsibility of the OG Sibenik. Within the framework of the OG Sibenik, they were active even during the first couple of days, and they covered the area of responsibility of the region of Drnis and around Drnis. That was the way how things were co-ordinated between those two units. Those two units were linked up, and they worked together, in concert. As far as co-ordination is concerned with the civilian police, the civilian police also had certain units, if we wanted to use military terms, and they were tasked with establishing police stations in most of the bigger settlements that had been liberated, and that form of co-ordination happened daily and involved the commanders of the units of military police and the commanders of the police stations that had been established in that area. My role was to establish whether that co-ordination evolved on a daily basis, whether it was effective, and whether there were possibly some problems that we could deal with at other co-ordination levels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Just to check whether I understood you well, is it like, You'll go there and cover this area, or, You establish a police post here, whereas we will do that; is that the kind of co-ordination to divide tasks and to see that no double work was done, and that as effectively as possible the area was covered by the activities of the 72nd and 73rd? Is that how I have to understand your -- could you give us, perhaps, one clear decision where you said, This is a decision I took in the context of co-ordination, just by way of an example?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: You mean the civilian police, the military police, or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's start with the 72nd/73rd.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: We can say that one part of the area of responsibility that was covered by the 73rd in Drnis was covered by certain activities, which means that we looked at the number of check-points, the number of patrols, and the areas that certain patrols covered during their regular patrols. And this was all aimed at relieving those units that were over-worked and had too much to do, and we wanted to distribute the burden evenly between the 72nd and the 73rd Battalions of the Military Police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And now an example of co-ordination between civilian and military police.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: I personally -- when I went either to Obrovac, or Benkovac, or Drnis, or when I was in Knin itself, I personally checked on a daily basis with the members and commanders of the military police, maintained the regular co-ordinations with members of the civilian police, and this was all to do with manning check-points, whether they would be manned by the military police only, by the civilian police, or whether they would be manned jointly, or how we would co-ordinate the work and activities of both the police forces in that area where they were responsible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. In the context of this co-ordination, did you attend meetings of high-level authorities, and I'm now -- whether that would be meetings purely within the military context, or with civilian authorities, or MUP authorities?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Those were mostly co-ordinations with the commanders of the police stations that had been organised in the liberated areas. I can't remember, but perhaps somebody from the Police Administrations also attended those co-ordination meetings, but nobody above them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This Chamber received evidence, a witness who told us that you attended a high-level meeting -- and for the parties, I'm referring to transcript page T-8973 -- that you attended high-level meetings to agree on the work, and that you would then provide this witness, who was also working in the military police, as to how the task that had been agreed upon should be carried out. So it describes, more or less, you attending a meeting with -- high-level meetings, and he was talking about co-ordination between military police and civilian police, and then give further instructions down the line.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour. Could you please jog my memory? What meeting are you referring to, and where did that meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not referring to a specific meeting. I'm referring to the evidence this Chamber received, and let me just check for one second. I'll try to find the place where the witness -- I am trying to find exactly what he said. He was talking about you, as a co-ordinator, and he said the following: "He co-ordinated the work of the military police and the work of the civilian police. He attended high-level meetings to agree on the work, and then he would provide me ..." And the witness was a company commander in the 72nd Battalion -- Military Police Battalion: "... and then he would provide me with guide-lines as to how the task that had been agreed on should be carried out." So there are no further details. That's the reason why I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really can't remember a meeting attended by high officials of the Ministry of the Interior and us, discussing operational matters during Operation Storm. I really don't know. Was that some other kind of meeting, a meeting of a different nature? That may well have been the case, but I really can't remember officials of the Ministry of the Interior -- high-ranking officials of the Ministry of the Interior attending a meeting that I, myself, also attended, and that meeting dealing with operational matters, on top of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as your recollection goes, what was the highest level of meeting you remember to have had with MUP officials when you were in the area between the 3rd and the 13th of August?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: I believe that the chief of the Police Administration of Sibenik and Knin was the one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you ever attend meetings where Mr. Cermak was present?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And who else were present at those meetings? Were MUP officials present, were others present? Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I attended perhaps one or two meetings that General Cermak organised. However, those meetings were attended by large groups of people. I remember that we could not even find seats in the largest room that we had. There were representatives of the civilian police, the military police representatives were also there, and I believe that there were also representatives of some international organisations, perhaps the UN or some others. I don't know. I really can't remember the composition of people who attended that meeting, but I remember a large crowd. That's what I remember very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Juric, we'll first have a break, and we'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Juric, I'll move to a new subject, that is the reporting system, primarily. When you were posted in Sector South in the period I mentioned before, did you report to General Lausic on issues of crime?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could your microphone be activated? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The system of reporting that had been established was as follows: I was at the forward command post of the -- the commander of the 72nd Battalion of the Military Police that had operative duty service, and that is where reports came from all subordinate units. Either I or one of my colleagues would draw up a single report on the basis of the information received from the subordinate units, and in accordance with General Lausic's orders, we sent this to Zagreb, to the Military Police Administration, up to 2000 hours every day, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You only did send those reports to the Military Police Administration, Zagreb, or were there any other addressees?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I only sent my report to the Military Police Administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, apart from the system of reporting - we'll come back to that at a later stage - would the occurrence of crime be subject of reporting if it would have happened?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. Everything we got from the subordinate units by way of reports or information, that would be included in any report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In your previous answer, you said that reports came from all subordinate units, and then you would -- you or your colleague would draw one single report. Would you include any information you gained by your personal observation of what you saw in the field?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, yes, I would. Also, I would usually call the Military Police Administration on the phone, and I would inform them about all the knowledge I had, personally, that had to do with the implementation of tasks or some problems that I had observed during the course of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that then not appear in the written report, what you told them by phone?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, if I were personally present when the report was being written up. However, I thought that written reports and oral reports had the same value, the same significance, the same importance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us an example of some personal observation, which you included in the report, which you had not seen in the reports by the subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot remember specifically. I cannot remember any specific matter that I perhaps did or did not include in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I take you to some of the reports which you may have received. Could we have a look at P1193. And I'd like to go to page 9 in the English, 7 in the B/C/S. Yes, the second paragraph I'd like to have highlighted. Yes, that one. That seems not to be page -- is that page 7? Let me have a look. One second, please. Apparently we do not have the right page in B/C/S. Let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, in the B/C/S it is on the screen. It's the third paragraph on the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the third paragraph. Oh, then I made a mistake. My apologies for that. Yes, I see the "five to six." Yes, it's my mistake. Mr. Juric, could you please read the last paragraph of your page in B/C/S? This, apparently, is a report on the events of the 5th of August. Do you remember whether you received this report of five to six bodies being found during searches, and then security services being informed? And then it says: "Considering the shortness of time passed since our entrance into the city, we assumed that these were people of Croatian ethnicity who had been killed by Chetniks." Do you remember that you received such a report?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot say with 100 per cent certainty whether I received it or not. However, if that is the report that was sent by the military police of Benkovac on that day, then most probably it did arrive at the centre there and that we read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, reading that, five to six people being killed, easily assumed that these were Croatians killed by Chetniks, you considered, I think, that no serious crimes were reported to you. Would you join the conclusion here that exclusively on the basis of timing, that this must have been Croatians killed by Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I did not draw any conclusion on this basis, either then or would I do so now. This is a report that was compiled on the 6th of August. That is to say, it was related to the 5th, the 5th, 6th, that's right. That is to say that fighting was still going on, intensive fighting in the area. This report clearly shows that members of the military police found five or six dead persons there, and they certainly informed those who they were supposed to inform about that. And the documentation of the military police would certainly have to have this, and especially the crime military police that was in charge of going out into the field, on the scene, doing their part of the work. I mean, we did not take into account this allegation and opinion of the person who wrote the report and stated his personal view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you give any instructions as to the persons that were found to be identified so that you could establish whether or not the assumption expressed in this report had any factual basis?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Yes. As you could see, members of the crime military police and members of the general military police were with me on this team. All of them received precise and clear tasks down their own line of work. One of the tasks of the crime military police was precisely that; namely, that all persons that are found -- all the bodies that are found should be dealt with appropriately, as usual, by the crime police, and if they cannot do that, they should inform, as soon as possible, the closest civilian police unit that should record that, and they should do whatever should be done, in professional terms, in such cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're now talking in general terms. But in relation to this report, were any orders given such as, Take care that the bodies are properly identified? Do you have any recollection of taking such action?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: As I read this report and at the time, I certainly would give such guide-lines, either I or somebody who was duty operations officer, or whoever was present at the time from the crime military police. That was regular procedure. It wasn't anything extraordinary, to give that kind of task and to have that kind of thing done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is, again, an answer in general terms that this is what would be done or would usually. Is there any documentation, any record of giving such instructions in this case, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I'm not sure whether there are any kind of records and whether I, myself, issued any tasks in relation to this particular case. However, I repeat once again, Your Honour, that at any rate, for such cases tasks to have this done had to be given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, in this report it appears that if there were any such instructions, that on a loose assumption based on timing only, one would not investigate?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with all due respect, the regular tasks that were carried out and the way in which this was carried out involved such cases as regular cases that had to be recorded and that had to be processed. Once again, I repeat, perhaps the person who wrote up this report was not educated enough and, therefore, gave his own views here, but those were the tasks of the members of the military police, and checks were made as to whether tasks were being carried out properly. And I can say with certainty that this had to be recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take you to the next page in B/C/S, and, in English, the same page, last paragraph. There, it is reported that: "It should be emphasised that only one fire incident occurred in the town itself ..." Do you have any recollection of this part of this report? This is the report by Mr. Kranjcevic, and it is about Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: If that is what is written in this report, then I accept that that was reality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This is reported by the military police, but we do not see any indication of the matter be investigated. Did you receive reports or were there instructions that if houses were on fire, that it should be investigated, what caused the fire?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can just engage in guess-work to the effect that the members of the military police who came across this obviously did not find anyone around that house, and, therefore, nothing was written in the report itself. In case they had noticed anyone, if they had noticed some persons in the vicinity, that certainly would have been intimated in this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you agree with me that at least the matter is considered in the context of possible arson or torching of houses, because the report says there were no attempts of house-torching and that the situation was satisfactory?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Yes. But what was particularly highlighted there is that it was noticed that a house was in flames and that measures were taken for the fire to be put out as fast and as efficiently as possible in order to prevent possible spread of damage. I do not see that any attempt was made to conceal or hide anything that had happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to take you a little bit further down in this document; page 10 in English, page 8 in B/C/S. Could you please read the third full paragraph from the bottom in your language, and forgive me for the pronunciation, starting with: "Treba napomenuti."

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I've read it, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Here, it is described that the problem started in the locations from which the military police withdrew in order to go to the front-line, and that places were left without military policemen, and that that complicated the work for the MUP, that there was a manpower shortage. Do you remember to have received such report?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is one of the statements that appeared almost every day in co-ordinations and talks among us, members of the military police, and when we had our joint co-ordination meetings with MUP members. Our area of responsibility was quite large. We were under-staffed. People worked for 12 hours, and then they were off for 12 hours. We tried to do as much as possible in order to cover as much of the area of responsibility and be present as much as we could. You know that it's very difficult to cover a relatively large area of responsibility if you're seriously under-staffed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll further look at some of the reports at a later stage, but I'd just touch upon another matter meanwhile. Would the commanders of the 72nd and 73rd Military Police Battalion, who reported to you, would they also report to General Gotovina, or would they receive any reports from military commanders? I'm interested to know what the reporting links, either receiving or sending, were between the military HV operational command and the military police.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: The practice continued, the customary practice of the military police. The highest-ranking commander in an area of responsibility, who was the operative commander, was supposed to receive daily operative reports from military police units, and that had, indeed, covered all the developments in the corresponding area over the period of 24 hours. Also, those commanders were supposed to be present at the briefings that operative commanders in their respective areas of responsibility held. At those briefings, they were supposed to receive certain information -- or, rather, they were supposed to be briefed and they were supposed to provide briefings to others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you also report -- apart from to the Administration of Military Police in Zagreb, did you report to also non-military police, military commanders? And if so, to whom did you report?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I sent my reports only to the Administration of the Military Police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber received evidence that there was a reporting system along two different chains of commands; that is, both in the HV hierarchy and in the military police hierarchy. I do understand that you say that is not what happened. Were you supposed to report in the HV hierarchy? Yes?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I didn't say -- if I understood your question well, I didn't say -- in the introductory part, I said that the reporting system followed the old system, as it had been established in the military police, which means that commanders were duty-bound to report to the operative commanders at the highest level of the developments that had taken place. And I, personally, I was duty-bound to report only to the Administration of the Military Police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you then tell us -- apparently, if I understand your answer well, other military police commanders, they would report to -- well, within the HV hierarchy. Could you tell us to whom the commanders of the 72nd and 73rd Military Police Battalion would report in the military HV hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: The commander of the 72nd Battalion of the Military Police needed to receive a summary of security developments, and he was supposed to send it to the commander of the military district.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did that happen?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But your responsibility for the performance of all tasks within the military police would not include any responsibility for appropriate reporting within the HV hierarchy, or to supervise that and to check whether that happened?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was an established procedure which started or was launched at the moment when the military police was organised and when the Rules of Service of the Military Police were introduced and continued thereafter, so I did not need -- I did not feel the need to check whether those rules were being implemented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave this subject, Mr. Juric. Did you become aware, when you were posted in Sector South, of burning and looting committed by HV members in the town of Kistanje and the surrounding villages on or around the 6th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I was in Kistanje personally on the 8th or the 9th -- I can't remember when it was. It was either on the 8th, the 9th or the 10th. I inspected a small group of the military police which had been sent there pursuant to a special order in order to provide security for an Orthodox monastery and a factory which was a special-purpose factory, as we called it, which means that it manufactured some military equipment or materiel. And as I arrived in Kistanje, I did not notice anything that would be out of the ordinary, and I didn't notice anything that fell out of the scope of regular combat activities. At the moment when I was there, I am certain that I did not see a single house burning at that moment, and I saw some four or five destroyed houses that could have been destroyed during the war. And as far as I can remember, on that day, in passing or in Kistanje, itself, I saw UN members who were present on that day, on the same day I was there, and there was nothing going on on that day, nothing out of the ordinary, nothing that would suggest anything of the kind you indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have P203 on the screen, the first page both in English and B/C/S. Could you please focus on the paragraph starting with: "In the liberated areas of the hinterlands of Zadar and Sibenik ..." This is a report from Mr. Gugic of the SIS, the Security and Information Services, to Gojko Susak and Miroslav Tudjman, and I read the relevant part. He says: "More precisely," and the report is dated the 8th of August, "in the liberated settlements Bribirske Mostine, Djeverske and Kistanje, the situation is rather chaotic. Incidents of mass burning of houses, plundering of property, alcohol consumption occur, and the units lack organisation." That does not match, apparently, with your observations. Do you have any explanations, where you said, There wasn't even a house burning, I didn't even see a house burning, that apparently the assessment of Mr. Gugic is quite different?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I said that I was in Kistanje on that day, and I really did not see any of that. I don't know what was going on in other places. I was not there, so I can't tell you anything about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, this report continued to say that this was reported by the -- was reported to the commanders of the operational groups, and it then continues: "A military police platoon has been assigned to the area in order to normalise the situation concerning the HV members." Which seems to fall within the scope of your responsibility, that is, giving tasks to military police platoons. Did I understand you well, that -- let me just check -- that you had a different reason for military police being sent there to provide security for an Orthodox monastery and a factory which was a special-purpose factory? That's not what Mr. Gugic reports. He says that it was to normalise the situation concerning the HV members.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: I've spoken about the military police in Kistanje. This had been planned and agreed, and they were sent to Kistanje without any information about anything happening in Kistanje. It was our task to secure the two or three facilities that were there. I can't remember the date when that military police unit was sent to Kistanje. Whether that unit was recognised by Mr. Gugic as a unit that had been sent to normalise the situation, I wouldn't know. In any case, that unit that was billeted in Kistanje was also tasked with securing public peace and order in the area of responsibility that was assigned to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said you visited the area. The Chamber received evidence that you would have visited the area on the 9th of August. Does that match with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I said that on the 8th and 9th and 10th, I toured the area, but I can't give you a specific date. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, others who were present in that area reported that on that day when they saw you in that area, that they went through Kistanje, which was totally destroyed and smelled of bodies. Do you -- that also does not match very much with your recollection, does it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can only repeat that on the day when I was in Kistanje, I did not see a single house burning. I did not notice a single body or anything that you have just indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One of those who had seen you in that area on that day was asked whether you were aware of the situation. I'm referring to the testimony of Mr. Hill; transcript page 3849 and 3850. And he said, Absolutely. And perhaps I add to that that in that area, on the 9th of August, another person went to that area and said that he encountered -- had an encounter with you in Kistanje municipality, and that you would have asked him what they were doing in a restricted area, that you gave them food, and that you then told them to return to the UN compound. Does that trigger any recollection as to the encounters you may have had? And as you said, you did see representatives of the international community when you went to Kistanje.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I said that on the day I was down there, I spotted a member of the Canadian military police on the road. I stopped, I invited them to come and visit us. I never hindered their movement across the area of responsibility. I never forbade them to move around. On the contrary, we had received an order to allow them and enable them maximum freedom of movement across the entire area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, apparently your recollection is different from what that witness told us. He said that later on that day, they drove through the town of Kistanje and that they had to close the windows of the car because of the heat emanating from the burning buildings. Did you ever observe or receive reports about, on the 9th of August, still burning buildings in Kistanje?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether I received a report about what you are describing, but let me repeat, once again, that all -- on the day, at the moment when I was there, not a single house was ablaze, and these are the facts. That's what I noticed or didn't notice on the day when I was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that if houses would have been in flames, that it may have been very difficult to miss that, to not observe that, if that was the case?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, of course, the Chamber is still puzzled by the fact that some persons saw houses burning, and there were even reports of HV soldiers going to houses and then those houses being in flames briefly after that, that we are puzzled by the fact that you apparently did not observe anything; whereas reports from internationals, but also a report by Mr. Gugic on the 8th of August, give a totally different picture on matters which you almost could not have missed to observe if they were there. Could you assist us in resolving this puzzle?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the commander of the Canadian military police was present there and if I was there, I don't know how many other military police officers were there. Also, I believe that maybe two or three Canadian police officers were also there. Would we have been sitting together or standing together in the middle of the road, and would we have been watching houses burning without doing nothing? I'm sure that I would have done something. I would have gone there, and I'm absolutely sure that the Canadians would have also behaved the same. I repeat, once again, I don't know when I was there. I don't even know what time of day it was. But when I was there, I did not see a single house ablaze at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was there any specific reason why you went to Kistanje on this day, which is by others reported as being the 9th of August?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I've already told you that we had received a task to send some of the military police officers there to secure those facilities, and I went to check how the task was being implemented. I wanted to see whether the men did their job, whether they were well equipped, whether they were well informed and briefed about the task, and whether they were performing their basic task, the one that they were there for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you remember when for the first time a military police platoon was sent to Kistanje?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: I don't remember, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I would tell you that a duty officer log-book reported that on the 6th of August, at 20 minutes to 9.00 p.m., military policemen were sent to Kistanje, would you have any reasons to doubt the accuracy of such an entry in the log-book?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you remember what specific purpose was served by sending a platoon? Was that just to protect the Orthodox monastery or -- and the other facilities, or are you aware of any other reasons? I'm asking you this also in the context of the report by Mr. Gugic and by the observations of others, but limiting myself to Mr. Gugic, who already on the 8th of August observed the chaotic situation, mass burnings, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: I know that before Operation Storm started, the company in Sibenik had the task of securing particular facilities at the moment when the members of the Croatian Army liberated the area. That was the plan, and that is why my military police unit went to Kistanje. Now, whether in the meantime the task of that unit was changed and whether anything else changed, I cannot recall at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you reported to General Lausic about events the 9th and the 10th of August, in which report no mentioning is found at all of any mass burning and/or looting. In your report of the 10th of August, if you'd like to see it, but to see that there's no mentioning there of something, if you'd like to look at it, it's fine, but I think that the parties and the Chamber agree that there's not such a report on mass burning or looting. However, in the report of the 10th of August -- and perhaps we could have a look at that, and that is D733. Could we have that on the screen. In item 2 of this report, it's mentioned that the members of the unit are still guarding the two industrial facilities and the Orthodox monastery. Here, again, if Mr. Gugic reports about mass burning, if two internationals are describing, with some detail -- any problems in receiving translation? Do you receive translation at this moment?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, it is surprising that those who are guarding a monastery and other facilities would have missed such information as extensively described by the internationals and being in accordance with earlier observations by the SIS. Do you have any explanation for that, that where you may have missed, if it was there, the burning and looting, why those who were stationed there would have missed that as well?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, as regards my reports that I received from the units and then sent to the chief of the Administration of the Military Police, I described what I learned. Whether there was a special report about Kistanje or apparently about Kistanje on the 10th, I don't know, I can't remember. However, if there had been a lot of arson and burning, I'm sure that members of the military police should have reported that, either in a regular report or an interim report, and I really don't know how that was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's move on. I just told you that no reference to burning or looting was found in the reports of the 9th and the 10th of August. The days prior to that, do you remember whether reports were sent as you were supposed to do, that is, reports on what happened on the 6th, the 7th, and the 8th, because - and I'm now looking at the parties - such reports are not in evidence, from what the Chamber could find. Could you tell us whether such reports were made and sent?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: It is quite certain that we wrote reports every day, and it is quite certain that we sent those reports. I don't know. I don't understand how come they couldn't be found anywhere in the archives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you say they must have been there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: That's right. It is quite certain that we compiled them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On a daily basis also for the 6th, the 7th, and the 8th?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber looked into the reports that are in evidence, the reports you sent to General Lausic. Nothing in those reports is said about any burning and/or looting in the town of Knin. Could you tell us whether this was ever reported, because, as you know, we've seen some reports and evidence, but apparently some reports are missing. Did you report any burning and looting ongoing in Knin?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Yes. In addition to this report, the members of the crime military police sent separate reports every day along their own line.
