I cannot remember right now whether that was in writing or orally. However, at any rate, I do know that such incidents were reported and that superiors were informed about such incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say these incidents were reported and superiors were informed. Was there any other action taken?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: I cannot say specifically against how many persons military police initiated proceedings and filed criminal reports, or against how many persons had disciplinary reports filed against them to the Military Court, but certainly there were such reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were people arrested for those purposes, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, did you report this to General Lausic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: About what, specifically, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: About looting ongoing in Knin, burning, perhaps, in Knin ongoing.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: It is quite certain that I informed him about all of the incidents that occurred throughout the area, not only in the area of Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And was that in your reports?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. About those that I knew of and those that I found out about through the channels of regular communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would those be in your written reports?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall whether everything was recorded in the written reports, because written reports were compiled by the Operations Duty Service and I could not always reach them. But, at any rate, I informed the Military Police Administration by telephone of all the knowledge that I had and everything that I had received by way of reports in my area of responsibility from the units there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, on the basis of the 2nd of August order, you were tasked with reporting, which reports would include, and I quote: "The status of crime in liberated areas and in zones of combat operations, number of crimes, crime reports filed, and escort of HV members who committed crimes." To report this by telephone looks quite uncommon, because giving such details by telephone, names, numbers of reports -- do you have an explanation, or was this reported in writing?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: As for this telephone conversation of mine and that way of reporting, it was mostly in general terms. I did not report on names or specific cases. In written reports, that had to be referred to more specifically. I don't know whether, in addition to these reports, there are reports where members of the military who were in the same group that I was in reported about this. I don't know. I simply do not remember how or in which way -- well, how come some things are not in this report. Were they sent through some other report? Obviously, perhaps on that day units had not reported anything to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we address the parties. These reports of the 6th, 7th -- covering the 6th, the 7th, and the 8th, are they available anywhere? Because we have seen the 5th of August, we've seen the 9th, the 10th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We haven't been able to locate the 6th and the 7th. I will check to see if we have it for the 8th, to check to see if it's in evidence, because I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It may be that we -- in our searches, that we missed something. Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: We don't have reports for those days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't have reports for those days. I would like, then, to move on. The next subject I'd like to ask you some questions about, Mr. Juric, is about the relations between the military police and its responsibilities in relation to civilians. Could you tell us, what exactly was the role of the military police in relation to civilians that were found when you were there in Sector South?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: The military police had a twofold role in this respect. As for all civilians that would be found within the combat area, they were supposed to evacuate them as soon as possible and as efficiently as possible and hand them over to the civilian police that was organising the collection centres. As for finding civilians in the area of responsibility, exclusive authority in the zone that does not belong to classical combat, it is the civilian police that had that authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do you consider "combat area"? I mean, if you moved in together with the troops and if there would have been no resistance or no resistance anymore, would you then still have to evacuate the civilians?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know what I can answer specifically at what point the zone of combat activity stops or starts. At any rate, at the moment when the units of the Croatian Army liberated a particular locality, and when relative peace was established, the units of the military police and civilian police relatively soon came to that area, so I can say that practically at the same time all units of the civilian police and all units of the military police would arrive within a liberated area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would they stay in the collection centres, these civilians?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of that, Your Honours. I don't know how it was organised later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's say just before you left, 11th of August, perhaps 12th of August, would there be any reason to keep civilians in the collection centres?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know how to answer this question. Not all civilians were in collection centres. There were civilians who were -- well, when we're talking about Knin, itself, there were some civilians who were within the UN camp. Part of the civilians were in the areas of Sinj and Sibenik. I think that at the moment when all kinds of combat activities stopped, in a way, it should have been possible for those civilians to go back home. I don't know how that was done and in which way. That was not within the scope of authority of the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, nevertheless, the presence of civilians in reception centres was part of reports by the military police. Does the name of Mr. Glavan --

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he was an officer who was with me on the team, and he was responsible for the work of the crime military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And he reports about civilians in reception centres. You said it was not within the scope of the military police. Nevertheless, it's part of a report dated the 11th of August by Mr. Glavan.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Perhaps he wrote how many people from the war zones was handed over to the civilian police, whereas you asked me how and in which way they were received in these centres and when they were supposed to be released from the centres. My answer to that was that I was not aware of that part of the activities involved. However, I know that all were transferred to a safe place from the combat areas. Maybe it's that that Mr. Glavan is reporting about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Glavan gives the numbers of people, both prisoners of war in collection centres but also the number of civilians at present, the 11th of August, in reception centres, so he does not report on handing over. If you'd like to have a look at this report during the next break, I'll be glad to give it to you so that you can -- would you like to have a look at it and see whether there's any further comment on your part?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, no. No, I'm quite sure that my colleague Mr. Glavan, in his report, speaks of the total number. Now, whether it's military persons or civilian persons who were transferred from the war zones, or if we're talking about prisoners of war who were transferred for their own safety, so that they would get out of the war zone as soon as possible, and that these people, in a way, went through the hands of the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll briefly deal with one last subject before the break. As far as you're aware of, were the units of the 72nd or the 73rd Military Police Battalions ever engaged in guarding cemeteries?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, this Chamber heard evidence in relation to the 6th of August, and I'm referring to P875 [Realtime transcript read in error "P785"], and I quote from that statement: "Some of my military police were involved in the guarding of the Knin Cemetery, together with the civilian police." Does that in any way refresh your memory or are you not aware?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall, Your Honour. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In that statement, the person gives as the reason that it was in order to protect those who were burying the bodies. Does this trigger any thoughts on the task of the military police in protecting those who were burying bodies? Is there anything in your recollection which would tell you anything about, if such a task was performed, when it would have been handed over to the civilian police again?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently the whole matter does not --

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. No, Your Honour. I can say with 100 per cent certainty that I do not remember any such thing having happened or that I knew in any way that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then have a break first. We'll resume at 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber was informed, Mr. Carrier, that you would like to address the Chamber before the witness comes in.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just very briefly. Today, you put to the witness that in August 2nd -- or he was tasked with reporting, and went through some criminal reporting. I'm assuming you referred to D844, and it's not clear from that document whether it was ever sent to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether I was referring to that document. I can tell you what I was referring to -- let me have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think it's D267, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I think I referred to 2D844.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Yes, and, Mr. President, just looking at that document, and Mr. Misetic perhaps mirrors the confusion, it would seem that the August 2nd order that you have referred to before was D267 or D268, whereas D844 hadn't actually been sent to Mr. Juric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me have a look. D844 is sent by General Lausic and is addressed to the Command of the Military Police Detachment, 3rd Company, Zadar, 4th Company, Sibenik, and, fourth, Dubrovnik. So -- and then let me just see whether I find the same or similar language --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I can assist because I was going to do this in cross. The order from General Lausic to Mr. Juric --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- has not been admitted yet into evidence, and I was going to do that in my cross. It's 65 ter 2193.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any -- let's say the following. I put this to the witness, even if I referred to a wrong document, is there any dispute about whether he was supposed to report on the crime situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was going to show the witness that it was in D844 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- which was an order directly from Mr. Lausic to the 4th Company of the 72nd MPs. The substance of the report in D844 is the same as what Mr. Lausic issued in 65 ter 2193 to the officers he was sending into the field, just so there's no confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we -- do we have any problem in substance or is it just to correct me - I think you're right, Mr. Carrier - that I at least referred to a document which was not directly addressed to Mr. Juric?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I'd have to check the document that Mr. Misetic just referred to and make sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let's do that and see. If after cross-examination any matter remains, we'll then hear from the parties. And if I have been inaccurate in this respect, my apologies. I try, as you all do, try to be as accurate as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you. And just -- I apologise, just while we're on the subject of correcting things, in the transcript today, you referenced document -- or at least it showed up in the transcript, on page 52, line 21, as "P785," and I believe it should be P875.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge, I think Mr. Carrier is correct on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 785, and you say it should be 875. Yes. I intended to refer to P875.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. President, I understand that you had offered to have Mr. Juric look at an order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He seemed not to be very much interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No, clearly he wasn't interested, although I think what he was explaining was that he had received reports about civilians being handed over to -- by the MPs, and there are a number of reports, just for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not saying that this was not reported. I was just inviting him to look at this specific document I referred to. I remember that there are such reports which -- then anything else? If not, could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Juric, I'd like to ask you about any dealings you may have had with Mr. Cermak. Did he play any role in co-ordinating co-operation between civil and the military police?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cermak was appointed the garrison commander. He organised a couple of meetings. I've already told you that those meetings were attended by a lot of people who discussed a lot of things. General Cermak was not my superior. As the garrison commander, he did have the right to issue tasks to the military police in terms of implementing security details, checks, and similar things. However, I don't think that he played any major roles with regard to the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said he had a right to issue tasks to the military police. Could you tell us on what basis he had that right or that authority?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Duties, tasks, and whatever the military police had, in keeping with the rules. Every officer had the right to issue requirements and tasks that the military police then implemented if they were in accordance with the area of work and the authorities of the military police. In that case, the military police were duty-bound to carry them out in the way prescribed by the scope of their work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber has received, although, a limited number of documents in which orders are given by Mr. Cermak and which were sent to the -- sometimes, among others, to the military police. I'd just like to put them to you to see whether you have any recollection. First - and for the parties it's D503, and I'd avoid to have everything on the screen again and again - in which General Cermak orders that a team, made up of members of the military police and personnel from the Knin police, should be set up with the task of finding the following UNCRO vehicles. Apparently, UNCRO vehicles had disappeared or had been stolen, and General Cermak orders setting up a mixed team, military police and personnel from the Knin Police Station. Do you remember such an order?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: I can't remember -- with 100 per cent certainty, I can't remember that order. However, if you say that it was drafted, then I'm sure that it was, which confirms what I've already said. General Cermak issued a task pursuant to a piece of information that he had received about a crime having been committed, and that the perpetrators had to be discovered. And in this case, as you have just said, some vehicles had been stolen. This certainly fell within the scope of the work of the military police, and the military police were duty-bound to accept that task and implement that task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, there is an order which is, to some extent, similar, dated the 12th of August, in which teams are ordered to be constituted to find equipment that apparently had been stolen or at least which was missing from UNCRO. Would that -- do you have any specific recollection of that? It's about earth-diggers and trucks and Land Rovers.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Just like before, I don't specifically remember any such order. However, obviously General Cermak received information from UN members, and then he shaped them as orders and issued them to the civilian police, and ordered them to find the perpetrators of such crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you consider this to be in the same range as the previous one we discussed and within the competence of Mr. Cermak; is that -- the previous one about the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Precisely so. This was not only within the competence of Mr. Cermak or General Cermak. The military police was duty-bound to receive any information, record that knowledge, and follow up on any such information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Earlier, you talked about tasks being given by Mr. Cermak to the military police. Do you consider this in the context of tasking or just informing?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: I would consider both cases as General Cermak having information that was not available to the civilian police, and that he issued an order -- or, rather, a task to follow up on such information. And both police forces had the authority to act upon such information and carry out the tasks issued to them with this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, another document - for the parties, I'm referring to D788 - contains what is written on paper as an order which is sent to the military police and the archives, not to any other police organisation, and which says, the order: "Control all entrances to the UNCRO barracks, including the main gate." And, second: "Particularly, checks are required when refugees leave the barracks. Do not allow them to leave without adequate authorisation." I don't want to go too much in the subject matter of the order, but did you consider this to be a kind of order or giving tasks, as you mentioned before, which was within the competence of Mr. Cermak, or did you not consider an order of this content to fall within that scope?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: General Cermak communicated directly with UN members who were billeted in the area of Knin. It seems that they had a conversation or talks as to how they would check the entry of people and their movement, and how they would protect the area. If an order was drafted in a way to give the military police authority to protect that area, that would have been within the scope of the military police. If they were asked to prevent people from exiting the area without any authorisation, that would also be within the scope of the work of the military police, and I personally don't see a problem there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And did you consider it within the competence of Mr. Cermak to give you, by this order, that task?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: I don't know the date, I don't know the context. Maybe you could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 8th [Realtime transcript read in error "2nd"] of August, 1995. The transcript reads "2nd." Perhaps I was unclear. It is the 8th of August.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Obviously, the general decided to refer that to the military police because that case involved army members in the region. Those were members of the UN who were there, and I believe that he was governed by that when he conveyed that information to the military police and not to the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If such an order was addressed to you, to guard the main entrance, was this also such an order which you felt duty-bound to follow?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: In terms of what I said previously, if that was to secure and protect an area of some military significance, which it was, indeed, in this case, I would see this as a regular military police task and I would implement that. I would carry that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In relation to freedom of movement both -- of UNCRO elements, we have seen an order -- at least a document with "Order" on it, dated the 8th of August, which was sent both to the Knin military police and the MUP, in which it is stated that all UNCRO elements with clearly-displayed insignia may move freely in the areas of Knin and Drnis. They are advised to use the main roads. Would this, as far as you are concerned, fall within -- would you accept this as an order which was given within the competence of Mr. Cermak and which you would feel that you'd have to follow?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As I've already stated previously, members had the freedom of movement. Namely, I received information, and I can't remember whether that was from the Administration of the Military Police or from somebody from the Ministry of Defence, that we were duty-bound to guarantee the freedom of movement to all UN members who were billeted in our area of responsibility. It was only after that, after that information was received and after I had issued a task to my units, that this particular order was issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say this order came at the moment where you had already prepared and organised the implementation of orders or information you had received previous to this order being issued by General Cermak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was privy to that information much before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is an order of the 8th of August which is addressed -- at least is sent to the military police and the Knin Police Station. The order -- the content of the order is that UNCRO helicopters must be inspected before each flight, and the inspection could be carried out by military police according to previously-submitted flight plans and in co-operation with UN and EU liaison officers. I leave alone other matters, such as movement of humanitarian convoys and the movement of UNCRO vehicles delivering food and equipment. I would like to focus on the first part, UNCRO helicopters being inspected. Is that -- first of all, is this 8th of August order an order you remember?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did -- as far as you know, did the military police ever inspect UNCRO helicopters before they took off?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Not in this form. We assisted security forces when VIP persons arrived in the region, and then we carried out anti-sabotage checks and similar checks. I don't remember this specific case that you've just described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Juric, you told us that if you were tasked in this way by documents which contain the word "order," that you felt duty-bound to do what you were tasked with. Was there ever any discussion about that, Do we have to do what Mr. Cermak asks from us or tasks us with? Was there any discussion ever, any dispute, about his authority to give you those tasks and you being duty-bound to perform them?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: I don't remember any specific discussions about that, and I also don't remember any tasks or General Cermak issuing anything in the form of order that would have contradicted the work and activities of the military police as described and regulated by the rules. In such a case, I'm sure that some of the military police members who would have received such an order would have come back to General Cermak, telling him that that was not within the scope and authority of the military police, and he would have also informed his superiors in the military police. And I'm sure that a decision would be made as to how to go on about implementing that particular task. You have to know that we were terribly under-staffed, and whenever people were assigned to carry out some tasks, that would have reduced the policing capacities and their ability to perform everyday tasks. And that was the number-one rule that guided us in our everyday work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like to move on to another subject. Military police patrols, would they be confined to the main roads and intersections and crossroads, or would they also go into the depth of the terrain, apart from the main roads?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Patrols mainly stuck to main roads for two reasons. We did not have enough vehicles or personnel at our disposal, and, on the other hand, there was a fear that much of the area was contaminated by mines. And for those two reasons, we could not have many patrols at the same time and we could not send them very far into the depth of the territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber received evidence that some of those who were still in active service would go home at night in their villages. Now, could you explain why it was safe enough for them to go to the villages, whereas you felt unsafe to go into the terrain? I'm now talking about smaller roads, villages, rather than the main roads. I'm not talking about going off-road.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: When I said "main roads," I meant asphalt roads, and we stuck to those. That was our principal work. Small auxiliary roads could not be covered, due to the lack of vehicles and lack of personnel. A lot of people, civilians and members of the Croatian Army, did want to go and check on their houses, and if they wanted to do that, they could not have been prevented by us, because they were more familiar with the terrain than us and it was their own responsibility that they went to check on their properties, on their houses and their farms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: And if you will allow me just one more thing. Please take into consideration the size of that area of responsibility, as opposed to the number of police officers that we had at our disposal, and how many check-points we had to man at all times in order to carry out that part of our responsibility. You will understand that we had very few people at our disposal, and we could not increase the number of our patrols and extend their working hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have a look at D1533, paragraph 12. Madam Registrar, just out of an abundance of caution, could you check whether there was any protection. If so, it should not be shown to the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have got two times the B/C/S on my screen, rather than one English and -- there we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I certainly don't have an objection, but I just want to make sure that I haven't missed any additional e-mails from Chambers about exhibits to be used with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It may be that we missed this one. That is, then, our apologies for that. I know that it was added at a late stage. And it makes the Chamber more humble in criticising not fully reporting, but if you'd have a similar forgiveness as you often show to each other, then the Chamber would highly appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. As I've said, obviously this is one we're very familiar with, but just in case there are any additional ones, it would be helpful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think so at this moment. Could you have a look at paragraph 12, and you see -- let me just check. No, I'd like you to look at the end of this paragraph, and we have to move slowly from this page into the English. It is about Brigadier Biskic issuing tasks to secure the depth of the area within the newly liberated territories. And then he lists a number of activities under A up to and including E. Could we move to the next page in English. You see some measures are indicated here. Could you please look at the last one: "... to travel only via the main roadways, to avoid side roads or short-cuts when travelling at night." The Chamber wondered, in this respect, how you could effectively secure the depth of the area when you primarily stay on the main roads.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Every day, every evening, we engaged in such small-scale analyses as to how we managed to cover the area. In essence, on the basis of the reports we received for the previous day, we would try to move blockade check-points, and somehow, in this way, to channel these small auxiliary roads to bigger roads, where we would actually have the checks. With the personnel we had available, we tried to do the best we could. When we changed the check-points every day and when we changed the directions involved, and when we changed patrols, we tried to ensure this presence. I don't know specifically whether at that particular meeting Brigadier Biskic presented these tasks, I cannot remember exactly, and whether it was stated specifically that we should not take small roads and paths during the night. But, at any rate, he was probably guided by the number of people available, the number of vehicles available, and the fact that quite a few of these very small roads had been mined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In this context and in this same statement, reference is made to something that happened on the 11th August 1995 in the area of Derala, where 20 members of the 141st Brigade of the Croatian Army were killed, as an indication of the danger going off the main roads. Could you tell us exactly, do you have any recollection of this event where over 20 members were killed?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. However, I don't remember the specific details involved and how this happened. I think that they were ambushed or something like that. I cannot say with 100 per cent certainty how that happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us, do you have any specific knowledge as to where Derala is? And what is it; is it a hill, a mountain, a village?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth right now, I really don't know. I cannot say. However, at the time of this particular information, I must have known roughly where it was, and it's quite certain that we would have looked it up on the map. As far as I can remember, one of the soldiers who got killed on that day there was related to Captain Glavan, who was on the team with me, and that's why I remember that particular event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did I understand from one of your previous answers, when we were talking about patrolling and the effectiveness of the measures taken, that the check-points were all, or most of them, on the main roads and intersections?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: I would not say that they were only on main roads. Our intent was to channel the smaller roads towards the main roads as much as possible, or, rather, those roads where we thought point B could be reached from point A, and in that way we thought we would increase our efficiency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you -- at the time when you were there, did you have check-points manned by civilian and military police? I think you earlier referred to that kind of co-ordination decisions. Did that happen, that the mixed check-points were set up, when you were there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Quite certainly, but I cannot tell you exactly now at which positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This Chamber heard evidence that uniformed police, and that was primarily civilian police, would not often visit villages which were situated at a distance from the main roads. Would the same be true for the military police?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot tell you with 100 per cent certainty, I cannot say yes or no. But, at any rate, whenever we received information that something was happening and when we were able to send a patrol, we would certainly do so, regardless of whether it had to do with a village that was on an asphalt road or beyond an asphalt road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Juric, the Chamber has at this moment no further questions for you. I'd like to -- I don't think that it makes much sense to start cross-examination at this moment, Mr. Carrier, five minutes before -- four minutes before we have to adjourn. Could the parties give us an indication as the time they would need, now knowing what the examination-in-chief has covered?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I hope to finish within the first session tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I hear from the Defence. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Then I would hope to finish within the second session tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Second session. Mr. Kay, don't tell me that you will hope to finish in the third session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It depends very much what goes before, but it would certainly be a session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I would have no questions, Your Honour, as the matter stands now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now we are at the -- tomorrow we have three sessions. Mr. Carrier takes one, Mr. Misetic takes another, Mr. Kay doesn't take less than one session. Mr. Juric, I am sure that the parties will do their utmost best to see whether we can conclude your examination tomorrow, but there's no guarantee for that. I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether that is the testimony you have given already or whether that's testimony still to be given tomorrow and perhaps on Monday. We'd like to see you back tomorrow, Friday, the 5th of March, 9.00 in the morning, in this same Courtroom III. We adjourn until then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
